Sampled responses: (80,496 × 13 + 19,680 × 12) × 10 = 12,826,080.
SUQ scores: (80,496 × 13 + 19,680 × 12) × 19 = 24,369,552.

Each SUQ measure evaluates a set of 10 sampled responses for one input and one model. The SUQ count is therefore per response set, not per individual response. These are protocol-derived totals, not an audit of completed generation or scoring logs.

The 33 settings comprise five QA datasets, two math datasets, four summarization datasets, and 22 translation directions: eight into English, six non-English to non-English, and eight English to multilingual. Input counts are summed across settings, without deduplicating related inputs across translation directions.

The two evaluation scopes overlap in model coverage. The 14-checkpoint union counts Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 and v0.3 separately. Additional sampled-model checks, temperature and backbone ablations, consistency baselines, and quality-metric re-evaluations are excluded from these totals.

Abstract

Semantic uncertainty quantification (SUQ) has become a central paradigm for detecting hallucinations in free-form language generation, as it measures uncertainty over meanings rather than surface forms. However, existing studies typically evaluate SUQ under limited tasks, models, and generation settings, making it difficult to understand when semantic uncertainty is reliable and where it fundamentally fails.

We investigate both questions through SURE, a large-scale empirical study treating SUQ as both an object of evaluation and a lens on LLM behavior. We compare 19 measures and variants from six studies across four tasks, 19 English-output datasets, and 13 LLMs, complemented by 12-model translation experiments across 14 non-English-target directions. First, we analyze Semantic Uncertainty itself: method rankings vary with task and simple consistency measures remain competitive in several evaluated settings. We identify SURE-OC, diagnostic subsets of low-quality generations assigned confidence, to characterize where semantic agreement and quality diverge. Second, we use semantic uncertainty to analyze LLMs: higher-performing models tend to exhibit lower uncertainty, including on low-quality outputs, while QA temperature sweeps show that better uncertainty separability can accompany worse answer accuracy. Together, the two perspectives distinguish the effectiveness of an uncertainty estimator from the behavior of the generator, revealing why lower semantic uncertainty alone does not establish greater reliability.

Why Study Semantic Uncertainty?

If a model keeps giving the same answer,
how much should we trust it?

Different wordings can express the same answer, and a fluent, consistent answer can still be wrong. SUQ measures variation in meaning across sampled responses. SURE asks how reliably those signals identify low-quality generations when the task, model, or output language changes.

Shared generations and semantic evidence make the method comparisons meaningful. Alongside the English-output tasks, translation into English, between non-English languages, and from English into multiple languages tests whether uncertainty estimates remain useful across language settings. The behavioral analyses of capability, overconfidence, and decoding focus on the English-output evaluation.

01 · Sample responses

Generate 10 responses for each model–input pair under a shared evaluation protocol.

02 · Measure semantic variation

Compare 19 SUQ measures and variants using shared sampled outputs and semantic evidence.

03 · Test reliability

Evaluate error ranking with AUROC/AUARC for QA and math, and quality ranking with PRR for summarization and translation.

What We Find

01 / TASKS AND LANGUAGES

Method rankings depend on what we ask models to do.

Strong performance on QA does not guarantee strong performance on summarization or translation. In the evaluated comparisons, simple consistency measures remain competitive, motivating semantic representations that retain partial agreement between longer outputs.

Multilingual translation. Across 12 models and 14 non-English-target directions, Discrete SNNE (only-denom) leads the 19 SUQ measures in ROUGE-L-based macro PRR for every model. Direction-level results are available in the Multilingual Translation category above.

02 / BLIND SPOTS

Semantic agreement can hide confidently wrong answers.

Repeated outputs can agree in meaning and still be wrong. SURE-OC provides model-specific diagnostic subsets for studying these low-quality, low-uncertainty generations. Same-family models show moderately greater overlap in these failures under the evaluated selection rule.

03 / MODEL CAPABILITY

Higher performance comes with lower uncertainty.

Higher-performing models tend to produce more semantically consistent responses. The relative uncertainty gap between low- and high-quality outputs shows a marginal decreasing trend, so lower semantic uncertainty alone does not establish greater reliability.

04 / DECODING BEHAVIOR

More detectable errors can come at an accuracy cost.

Increasing generation temperature can improve uncertainty-based error separation in QA while reducing answer accuracy. This trade-off depends on the task and model; it calls for evaluating generation quality alongside the uncertainty estimator.

Takeaway. Reliable uncertainty evaluation needs to account for the task, output language, and quality criterion. Semantic consistency is one piece of evidence about generation quality.

Source: SURE, Appendices H.2–H.3 (English-output tasks) and H.9 (multilingual translation) · QA/Math: AUROC · All translation and summarization: ROUGE-L-based PRR. Higher is better within each metric.
